desc:
Return the node values of a binary tree in inorder: everything in the left subtree (in inorder), then the node itself, then everything in the right subtree (in inorder). The empty tree gives the empty array.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] the answer is [2, 4, 1, 3]. For tree = [5, 8, 2, 7, -1, 4, 9] the answer is [7, 8, 5, 4, 2, 9].

The recursive solution is easy; the goal is to do it iteratively with an explicit stack.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: A node must be recorded after its whole left subtree, so you cannot record it when you first meet it.
Walk down the left spine from the current node, remembering every node you pass on a stack.
When you cannot go left any more, pop a node, record it, and continue with its right child (again going down its left spine). Stop when both the stack and the current node are empty.
editorial: Inorder visits the left subtree first, so you must first dive as far left as possible, keeping the nodes you pass on a stack: they are waiting for their left subtree to finish. When the current node is missing, pop the top of the stack. That node has its left subtree completed, so record it, then move to its right child and repeat the dive.

Each node is pushed once and popped once, so the running time is O(n); the stack holds at most one root-to-node path, which is O(height) and O(n) for a chain. This push-left-spine, pop, go-right loop is the template behind many other tree iterators (for example the binary search tree iterator), so it is worth knowing by heart.
